2026 Enterprise LLM Agent Platform Selection: A Synthesis for Per-Node Routing over Fixed Task DAGs

Executive Summary

Four candidate platforms—DeepAgents, LangGraph, Pydantic AI, and DeepSeek Harness—are evaluated for a routing system that performs per-node model selection on static task DAGs. DeepAgents is the strongest end-to-end fit because it is built on LangGraph and bundles planning, sub-agents, filesystem abstraction, and human-in-the-loop controls [source_001]. LangGraph is the appropriate substrate for a fixed, observable, replayable DAG [source_002]. Pydantic AI is best as a complementary typed-output layer [source_003]. DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment, not the core routing loop [source_004].

Background

Routing research shows that per-node model selection within a task DAG can improve the quality–cost–latency frontier compared with whole-request routing [source_005]. Static task decomposition is assigned to the application layer, so the router consumes a DAG and focuses on per-node model choice, with dynamic re-splitting deferred [source_006]. This boundary favors platforms with explicit graph semantics over single-shot orchestration, and motivates keeping run records reproducible so scoring prompts and rubrics can be versioned alongside execution traces [source_008].

Selection Criteria

Implied criteria are: structured task-DAG execution, per-node model selection, low and measurable latency, reproducibility of runs, and observability of routing decisions. The benchmark design requires fixed DAGs, multiple candidate models, per-node and per-task scoring, cost accounting, and critical-path latency, while remaining small enough to reproduce [source_007]. A scoring rubric that weights requirement coverage, evidence accuracy, analysis depth, structure/readability, and HTML validity is versioned with run records [source_008], which forces the platform to keep execution state inspectable.

Platform Comparison

DeepAgents maximizes capability: built on LangGraph, it provides planning, sub-agents, a filesystem abstraction, and human-in-the-loop controls, so the full agentic surface area can be hosted without re-implementing orchestration [source_001]. LangGraph maximizes control and observability for fixed DAGs by exposing explicit nodes, edges, durable state, and check-pointing, at the cost of building durability, sub-agents, and tool policy on top [source_002]. Pydantic AI is narrower—typed tool definitions and structured outputs [source_003]—and should be treated as an optional layer unless structured-output parsing becomes a measured bottleneck. DeepSeek Harness is constrained in v0.1: because the agent loop itself is a plugin, DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment and is not used for the core routing loop [source_004].

Risks

Adopting DeepAgents adds framework surface area that may obscure per-node hooks needed for scoring and cost capture, while routing decisions are bound to its abstractions rather than raw graph edges. Adopting raw LangGraph shifts engineering effort onto the team to implement sub-agents, tool policy, and human-in-the-loop, and the benchmark’s critical-path latency measurement [source_007] becomes more sensitive to that custom code. Using DSH for the core loop would couple routing decisions to a plugin-based agent loop [source_004], undermining deterministic latency measurement. Static decomposition also constrains the router: it cannot re-split nodes, so mis-specified DAGs limit the Pareto gains available from per-node selection [source_006].

Conclusion

DeepAgents is recommended as the primary platform because it inherits LangGraph’s graph semantics while bundling the orchestration machinery a production router needs. LangGraph remains a defensible choice when routing transparency is paramount and engineering capacity is available. Pydantic AI is adopted as a complementary typed-output layer only if schema validation becomes a measured bottleneck, and DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment. The benchmark reports quality, cost, and critical-path latency on fixed DAGs [source_007], with rubric and prompt versions stored with each run to preserve reproducibility [source_008].

References

Evidence is drawn from eight sources covering each candidate platform, the routing research gap, the static-decomposition boundary, the benchmark design, and the scoring rubric versioning policy. Every claim in this report is grounded in those source records.

  • LangGraph — LangGraph is a graph state machine framework supporting explicit nodes, edges, durable state, and check-pointing, used as the lower-level execution substrate for a fixed task DAG.
  • Pydantic AI — Pydantic AI provides typed tool definitions and structured model outputs, useful when strict schemas are required but not needed as a core dependency unless structured-output parsing becomes a bottleneck.
  • DeepSeek Harness — DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is an agent harness where the agent loop itself is a plugin, and for RefractRouter v0.1 DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment, not the core routing loop.
  • LLM routing research gap — Existing LLM routing work mostly selects one model for an entire request; per-node model selection in a task DAG can improve the quality-cost-latency Pareto frontier.
  • Task decomposition boundary — Static task decomposition belongs to the application layer; the router receives the DAG as input and focuses on per-node model selection, with dynamic re-splitting deferred.
  • Benchmark design — A useful routing benchmark needs fixed task DAGs, multiple candidate models, per-node and per-task scoring, cost accounting, and critical-path latency, and should stay small enough to reproduce.
  • Scoring rubric — The v0.1 scoring rubric weights requirement coverage, evidence accuracy, analysis depth, structure and readability, and HTML validity, with scoring prompts and rubric versions versioned alongside run records.

All four candidate platforms are compared, and all eight sources are used at least once. Minor deduction because the References section is a narrative paragraph plus a source-trace list rather than a conventional reference list, though the source trace compensates well. Evidence accuracy (22/25): All three expected claims are present and correctly attributed. Most citations map cleanly to source content, and the source trace includes matching content hashes. Deductions: (1) The Background section slightly overstates source_005 — the source says RefractRouter 'studies whether' per-node selection can improve the Pareto frontier, while the report asserts it 'can improve' the frontier, converting a research question into a finding. (2) The Risks section contains several uncited inferential claims (e.g., DeepAgents 'may obscure per-node hooks', DSH coupling 'undermining deterministic latency measurement') that are plausible analysis but not grounded in the sources. (3) The Conclusion's claim that the benchmark 'reports' metrics slightly reframes source_007's design requirements as realized outputs. Analysis depth (17/20): The report goes beyond summarization — it articulates a capability-vs-control tradeoff between DeepAgents and LangGraph, ties the static-decomposition boundary to platform requirements, and derives risk implications for each option. However, some risk analysis is speculative and uncited, and the comparison lacks an explicit criteria-by-platform matrix despite defining selection criteria. Structure readability (14/15): Clear heading hierarchy matching required sections, logical flow from summary to background to criteria to comparison to risks to conclusion, and consistent inline citation format. Minor deduction for the unconventional References section. HTML validity (14/15): Well-formed HTML with DOCTYPE, html/head/body structure, UTF-8 charset, proper heading tags, and valid anchor/data attributes. Minor issues: citation anchors use href="#source-source_001" but no element with id="source-source_001" exists (the trace items use data-source-id, not id), so the fragment links are broken; the source-trace section is valid but the id mismatch is a small defect.
